newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president takes political row to provinces.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president takes political row to provinces.

text.p: Embattled Belarussian President Alexander Lukashenko, lashed by opponents at home and abroad, took his political fight to his hometown but got a lukewarm welcome from his countryfolk on Friday.

As a political row escalated in the capital, Lukashenko, standing in the shadow of a statue to Soviet founder Vladimir Lenin in this eastern industrial town, appealed for support from a largely silent crowd of about 10,000 people.

"We cannot lose the referendum, because we cannot lose the referendum," he told crowds of factory workers, state employees, students and pensioners on Lenin Square to sneak a look at the 42-year-old former state farm boss.

"There cannot be a home, there cannot be a farm, there cannot be a nation without a master. There can be no orchestra without a conductor," Lukashenko, openly nostalgic for the Soviet Union, declared from the statue's platform.

"You mean like Yeltsin directed the orchestra in Germany?" one man scoffed, referring to an incident when President Boris Yeltsin bewildered onlookers by seizing a baton and conducting an orchestra during an official visit to Berlin.

Lukashenko, opposed by the constitutional court, parliament and Western officials who fear an emerging dictatorship, will ask the nation of 10 million to award him significant powers over all institutions in a referendum on November 24.
The crowd stood beneath flags daubed with identical slogans reading "Yes to the president's constitutional draft".
One man said: "We were sent here by our bosses".
"Our school is waiting for a command. Where are we to go?" asked a woman teacher waiting in line to enter the square and join the meeting, strongly reminiscent of stage-managed Soviet gatherings.

People in the crowd seemed to have joined the rally more out of curiosity than to express support for Lukashenko, who once ran a farm near their industrial town of 400,000 about 150 km (100 miles) east of the capital Minsk.

Lukashenko, whose economic policies have led to international lending bodies freezing credits to his country between Russia and Poland, scoffed at the idea of privatisation, which is racing ahead elsewhere in the former Soviet Union.
"They criticise me because 90 percent of enterprises are not privatised. But I think that is a great achievement," he said.

He referred indirectly to the political crisis in Minsk, where his security services barred the country's top electoral official, Viktor Gonchar, from his office on Friday. Lukashenko sacked him on Thursday for opposing the referendum.
"I am speaking here in Mogilyov and I don't know what the opposition will do now that I have sacked the head of the Central Commission on Elections and Referendums," he said.
He also urged people to take advantage of early voting -- which began on November 9 but is actually intended for those unable to turn up on November 24, according to the constitution.
"I urge you, whoever can, vote early. I don't know what else might happen there (in Minsk)," he said.

Lukashenko is seeking approval to extend his term by more than two years to November 2001, appoint half the constitutional court and half the electoral commission and to create an upper house of parliament partly named by him in the November 24 poll.
The Human Rights Watch-Helsinki monitoring group on Friday expressed concern at events in Belarus in a statement which said the referendum, if Lukashenko won, would be a "death knell for democracy".
